items.stem: A customer sends a dish back because it is too salty. Which way of deciding who should change their work matches backpropagation?

options.text: Start at the complaint and work backward, asking at each step how much that person's work affected the result.
options.feedback: Backpropagation passes blame backward from the loss, layer by layer, using what each step handed to the next.

options.text: Ask each person to change their work at random and see whether the complaint goes away.
options.feedback: That is closer to nudging each weight and running the whole network again, which is the costly approach backpropagation avoids.

options.text: Blame only the last person who handled the dish.
options.feedback: That ignores the earlier steps, and the earlier weights are exactly the ones that need a slope.

options.text: Ask everyone to change their work by the same amount.
options.feedback: Each weight affects the result by a different amount, so each needs its own slope.

items.stem: Before you try it: the network in the widget has six weights. How many of them connect directly to the output unit?

options.feedback: One connects each hidden unit to the output. The other four connect the inputs to the hidden units.
Four weights connect the two inputs to the two hidden units. The output unit has only two incoming weights.
Only the last layer of weights connects to the output. The rest connect earlier layers.
There are two hidden units, and each has its own weight to the output.

items.try: Press Step until the second Slopes line appears, and notice that the four earlier weights get their slopes from the blame passed back.

items.stem: A team needs slopes for a network with 2 billion weights. Method A nudges each weight and runs the network again to see whether the loss improved. Method B uses backpropagation. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Method A needs about 2 billion full runs for one step. Method B needs about one forward pass and one backward pass.
options.feedback: Backpropagation reuses numbers already worked out, so it gets every slope for about the cost of one forward pass.

options.text: Both methods need about the same amount of computing.
options.feedback: They differ by a factor of billions for a network this size.

options.text: Method A is cheaper, because it avoids the backward pass.
options.feedback: Avoiding the backward pass means repeating the whole forward pass for every weight.

options.text: Method B needs 2 billion passes, but each one is cheaper.
options.feedback: Method B needs one backward pass in total.
